newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Heating oil inventories seen not too bearish.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Heating oil inventories seen not too bearish.

text.p: The American Petroleum Institute inventory report for last week was less bearish for distillates than expected and lifted heating oil futures.
The rest of the report was broadly neutral, with gasoline getting back to 'normal' and crude also doing as expected for this time of year, analysts said.

"Everybody was expecting it to be negative for distillates and when you are expecting a bearish number and you don't get it the market is going to up," said John Saucer, industry analyst at brokerage Smith Barney in Houston.
Distillate inventories for last week were expected to have been up about 500,000 barrels, according to industry analysts and traders polled by Reuters.

The actual build was just over a million barrels, but traders instead chose to focus on the 748,000 barrel drawdown in heating oil stocks in the northeast U.S. (PADD I) and the cold weather which is expected to extend from the Midwest through the high heating oil-demand eastern states.
"I think that people are focusing more on the weather that is coming in rather than what happened to stocks last week," said Saucer.
Heating oil futures had a down day in expectation of a build, with January losing 1.28 cents to end at 73.54 cents a gallon. The contract came back up to just under 74 cents after the API report.
Nevertheless, the recent trend is clearly for continued high production and a narrower distillates shortfall.

Distillate output last week was down slightly but still running at nearly 3.6 million barrels, up from 3.3 million at this time last year. Last week's stocks were nearly 94 percent of last year's level, compared with a shortfall in recent months of 20 percent.
"I think the distillate stock increase is consistent with the prior two week's reports," said Tim Evans, an energy analyst at Thomson Research Group.
"Production is strong and seasonal demand hasn't really taken off just yet. Exports that had been a problem back in September have been absent in recent weeks and continue to be," Evans said.

In other sectors, gasoline production was back to a more typical 7.7 million barrels a day last week compared to the surge to 8.1 million bpd seen the previous week. Imports also settled back to 249,000 barrels from 342,000 barrels.
"The gasoline drop is constructive but i don't expect it to get a lot of price reaction. It is unlikely to signal a reversal of the seasonal pattern," said Evans.

Crude stocks also appear to be in seasonal spirit, with 4.6 million barrel drop in the PADD III Gulf Coast area probably linked to the usual end-of-year tax-related stocks drawdown in Texas. That draw was offset by builds in the east and Midwest to bring it to a national draw of around 2.6 million barrels.
